solution.concept_anchor: India's modification of USSR model — non-justiciability and citizen-only scope

statement_analysis.statement: Fundamental Duties in India were inspired by the erstwhile USSR Constitution, but the Indian Constitution departed from the Soviet model by making these duties non-justiciable.
statement_analysis.reason: The USSR Constitution (Article 59) contained justiciable duties. India borrowed the concept but made its duties non-justiciable — a deliberate constitutional modification.

statement_analysis.statement: Unlike certain Fundamental Rights that extend to all persons present in India, Fundamental Duties under Article 51A are restricted exclusively to citizens of India.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 51A expressly begins with 'every citizen of India', restricting duties to citizens. By contrast, rights under Articles 14, 20, 21 use 'person', extending to non-citizens.

statement_analysis.statement: Japan's Constitution served as the primary source of inspiration for India's Fundamental Duties, with India substantially replicating the Japanese model of constitutionally enumerated civic obligations.
statement_analysis.reason: The primary inspiration was the USSR Constitution's Article 59, not Japan's Constitution. While Japan's Constitution does contain duties, it was not the main model for India's Part IV-A.

solution.strong_distractor: d — All three appear plausible at first glance, especially Statement 3 which mentions Japan — a real comparative reference — making students uncertain about dismissing it.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct: USSR was the inspiration; India made duties non-justiciable — a confirmed departure from the Soviet model.
Statement 2 is correct: Article 51A's opening language restricts duties to citizens — confirmed by constitutional text.

Statement 3 is incorrect: Japan is a secondary comparative reference in constitutional scholarship. The primary source was the USSR, not Japan. India did not 'substantially replicate' the Japanese model.
Statements 1 and 2 are correct, Statement 3 is incorrect — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 uses Japan as the primary source — a 'scope-extension' trap. Japan is a real and relevant comparator in constitutional discussions of Fundamental Duties, giving Statement 3 surface plausibility. However, the primary inspiration is the USSR Constitution's Article 59, not Japan. Students who remember Japan being mentioned in this context without recalling its secondary/comparative role will accept Statement 3 as correct.
solution.final_explanation:
Understanding the constitutional borrowing behind Fundamental Duties requires distinguishing between the primary source, secondary comparators, and India's own modifications.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The erstwhile USSR Constitution's Article 59 listed duties of Soviet citizens. India borrowed this concept but removed justiciability — making Indian duties moral/civic obligations rather than legally enforceable commands.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Article 51A's explicit language — 'It shall be the duty of every citizen of India' — restricts the scope to citizens. Rights like Article 21 (life and liberty) extend to all 'persons', creating an asymmetry.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Japan's Constitution is a relevant comparative reference, but it was not the primary model for India's Fundamental Duties. The USSR Constitution (Article 59) was the primary inspiration. India adopted the concept selectively and modified it significantly through non-justiciability.

Value Addition:
• The USSR duties were binding legal obligations — India's non-justiciability is a significant philosophical departure.
• Article 12 of Japan's Constitution discusses duties of citizens in a rights-maintenance context — different conceptual framework from India's Part IV-A.
• Germany's Basic Law contains justiciable duties — a model India explicitly did not follow.

solution.concept_anchor: 51A(h) and 51A(j) — distinct intellectual vs aspirational duties

statement_analysis.statement: Article 51A(h) is the only Fundamental Duty with an explicitly intellectual and epistemic character, as it requires citizens to develop scientific temper, humanism, and the spirit of inquiry and reform.
statement_analysis.reason: No other sub-clause of Article 51A directly demands intellectual development or an epistemic disposition — 51A(h) stands alone in this regard among all 11 duties.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 51A(j), which calls upon citizens to strive towards excellence, is a redundant provision because its obligation is already subsumed within the broader intellectual duty of Article 51A(h).
statement_analysis.reason: Article 51A(j) addresses excellence in 'individual and collective activity' — a broader aspiration covering sports, arts, professions, and civic life, not limited to intellectual development. It has independent judicial citation value (AIIMS Students Union, 2001) and is not subsumed by 51A(h).

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who believe both 51A(h) and 51A(j) address intellectual/aspirational development may accept Statement 2's reasoning and choose option (a).
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is factually accurate: 51A(h) is uniquely epistemic/intellectual among all 11 duties. Statement 1 is correct.

Statement 2 claims 51A(j) is 'redundant' and 'subsumed' by 51A(h) — this is incorrect. 51A(j) covers excellence across all spheres of activity (sports, arts, civic work, professions) — far broader than and distinct from the intellectual/epistemic scope of 51A(h). It has been independently cited in AIIMS Students Union (2001).
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is a partial-truth trap: 51A(h) and 51A(j) do share an aspirational quality, making the claim that 51A(j) is 'subsumed' by 51A(h) superficially plausible. The error is in scope — 51A(h) is narrowly epistemic (scientific temper, inquiry, humanism) while 51A(j) is broadly aspirational (excellence in all activities). They are complementary, not overlapping. Students who blur this distinction accept Statement 2.
solution.final_explanation:
Articles 51A(h) and 51A(j) are distinct in scope and character, even though both have an aspirational quality.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 51A(h) is uniquely intellectual — it demands scientific temper, humanism, and the spirit of inquiry and reform. No other duty explicitly addresses the citizen's epistemic orientation. This is why 51A(h) is frequently the 'odd one out' in duty-classification questions.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Article 51A(j) requires striving for excellence in all spheres — individual and collective — covering sports, arts, professional excellence, civic participation, and more. This is far broader than 51A(h)'s intellectual focus. Furthermore, 51A(j) was independently cited in AIIMS Students Union v. AIIMS (2001) in the merit-versus-reservation debate — a judicial usage completely distinct from anything arising under 51A(h).

Value Addition:
• 51A(j) is the most open-ended duty — its breadth makes it applicable in diverse policy and judicial contexts.
• 51A(h) is the only duty relevant to anti-superstition legislation debates.
• NEP 2020 invokes principles aligning with both 51A(h) (critical inquiry) and 51A(j) (holistic excellence).

solution.concept_anchor: Structural features of Part IV-A — placement, obligor, non-justiciability

statement_analysis.statement: Part IV-A of the Constitution, containing Fundamental Duties, consists of only one article — Article 51A.
statement_analysis.reason: Part IV-A is the shortest Part of the Constitution, containing only Article 51A with its eleven sub-clauses (a) to (k).

statement_analysis.statement: Both Fundamental Duties (Part IV-A) and Directive Principles (Part IV) are non-justiciable, but Fundamental Duties bind citizens while Directive Principles bind the State.
statement_analysis.reason: This correctly captures the structural distinction: DPSPs are obligations on the State for governance; Fundamental Duties are obligations on citizens for civic conduct. Both are non-justiciable.

statement_analysis.statement: Part IV-A was inserted into the Constitution by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978, which reversed several provisions of the Emergency-era 42nd Amendment.
statement_analysis.reason: Part IV-A and Article 51A were inserted by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976, not the 44th Amendment. The 44th Amendment (1978) reversed several other provisions of the 42nd Amendment but did not create Part IV-A.

statement_analysis.statement: Fundamental Duties under Article 51A apply only to citizens, whereas some Fundamental Rights extend to all persons, including non-citizens lawfully present in India.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 51A's 'every citizen of India' restricts duties to citizens; rights under Articles 14, 20, 21 use 'person', extending to non-citizens.

solution.strong_distractor: c — 'Only three' is the strong distractor: students unsure about Statement 3's attribution to the 44th Amendment might accept it, thinking the 44th Amendment made many changes to the 42nd Amendment's legacy.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct: Part IV-A has only Article 51A.
Statement 2 is correct: Both non-justiciable, different obligors — citizens vs State.
Statement 3 is incorrect: Part IV-A was inserted by the 42nd Amendment (1976), not the 44th (1978). The 44th Amendment reversed some 42nd Amendment changes but did not touch Part IV-A.
Statement 4 is correct: Duties are citizen-only; some rights extend to all persons.
Three statements are correct (1, 2, 4) — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 exploits the association between the 44th Amendment and reversals of 42nd Amendment provisions. Students who know the 44th Amendment undid many Emergency-era changes may assume it was also responsible for some aspect of Part IV-A, or may confuse which amendment inserted the Part. The precise fact — that the 42nd Amendment inserted Part IV-A and the 44th Amendment did NOT touch it — is the testable point.
solution.final_explanation:
Part IV-A's structural features are frequently tested through attribution, obligor, and single-article questions.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Part IV-A is the most compact Part of the Constitution — a single article (Article 51A) with eleven sub-clauses.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The DPSP-duty distinction is a foundational constitutional distinction. DPSPs (Part IV) guide State governance; Fundamental Duties (Part IV-A) guide citizen conduct. Both are non-justiciable.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The 42nd Amendment (1976) inserted Part IV-A. The 44th Amendment (1978) — passed after the Emergency ended — reversed some of the 42nd Amendment's provisions (restored pre-Emergency position on Article 352, 356, etc.) but left Part IV-A intact.
• Statement 4 — Correct: The citizen-exclusivity of duties creates a constitutional asymmetry with rights — some rights protect all persons, all duties bind only citizens.

Value Addition:
• Part IV-A is the only Part inserted wholesale by an amendment — Parts I through IV were original.
• The 44th Amendment specifically targeted Emergency-era changes to Articles 352, 358, 359 and the Lok Sabha term extension.
• No amendment between 1978 and 2002 altered Part IV-A.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 48A paired with Article 51A(g) — environment, parallel obligations
solution.strong_distractor: b — 'Article 47' is deceptive because Article 47 deals with health and nutrition (another environment-adjacent DPSP), making it plausible to students who recall Article 47 in the context of public health and living standards.
elimination_logic: The question requires identifying the DPSP provision that mirrors the environmental duty of Article 51A(g).
Eliminate (b): Article 47 deals with raising the level of nutrition, standard of living, and public health — not the natural environment.
Eliminate (c): Article 49 deals with protection of monuments and places of national importance — cultural, not natural environment.
Eliminate (d): Article 50 deals with separation of judiciary from the executive — entirely unrelated.

Retain (a): Article 48A, inserted by the 42nd Amendment, directs the State to protect and improve the environment and safeguard forests and wildlife — the exact DPSP counterpart to the citizen duty in 51A(g).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (b) — Article 47 — is the trap. Students know Article 47 deals with health and public welfare (which includes some environmental dimensions conceptually) and may substitute it for Article 48A, which is the precise DPSP dealing with natural environment protection. The entity-swap involves substituting a related but incorrect DPSP article for the correct one.
solution.final_explanation:
Article ________ of the Constitution directs the State to endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wildlife of the country, forming the DPSP counterpart to the citizen duty under Article 51A(g).

• Option (a) — Article 48A: Correct. This DPSP, inserted by the 42nd Amendment, is the State-directed obligation mirroring the citizen duty in 51A(g). Together they form a comprehensive constitutional environmental framework.
• Option (b) — Article 47: Incorrect. Article 47 directs the State to raise the level of nutrition and standard of living, and to improve public health — a health/welfare DPSP, not an environmental one.
• Option (c) — Article 49: Incorrect. Article 49 requires the State to protect monuments and places of national importance — a cultural heritage provision.
• Option (d) — Article 50: Incorrect. Article 50 concerns separation of the judiciary from the executive — structurally unrelated to environmental protection.

Value Addition:
• Both Article 48A and Article 51A(g) were inserted by the 42nd Amendment (1976) — simultaneous insertion for citizen and State.
• Courts read 48A and 51A(g) together in environmental PILs to establish a two-sided constitutional mandate.
• The Environment Protection Act, 1986 gives statutory force to both provisions.

solution.concept_anchor: Swaran Singh recommendations vs enacted duties — precise differences

statement_analysis.statement: The Swaran Singh Committee, constituted during the Emergency period, was the only body that has ever recommended the addition of Fundamental Duties to the Constitution of India.
statement_analysis.reason: The Swaran Singh Committee recommended the initial insertion of Fundamental Duties; the Verma Committee (1999) subsequently recommended implementation measures. More importantly, the 86th Amendment added a duty without any committee recommendation — the term 'only body' is incorrect.

statement_analysis.statement: All recommendations of the Swaran Singh Committee regarding Fundamental Duties were accepted and incorporated into Article 51A by the 42nd Amendment.
statement_analysis.reason: Several recommendations were not enacted: the duty to pay taxes, penal provisions for violations, and the committee's proposal for only 8 duties (10 were enacted). The adoption was selective, not wholesale.

statement_analysis.statement: The 42nd Constitutional Amendment, which inserted Fundamental Duties, is the amendment that also introduced the words 'Socialist' and 'Secular' into the Preamble of the Constitution.
statement_analysis.reason: The 42nd Amendment (1976) simultaneously inserted Fundamental Duties (Part IV-A) and amended the Preamble to include 'Socialist' and 'Secular' — both changes were part of the same sweeping amendment.

solution.strong_distractor: c — '3 only' is tempting because students who know Statement 3 is correct may stop their analysis there. The question asks which are NOT correct — requiring them to separately verify Statements 1 and 2 are both incorrect.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: 'Only body ever' — this is false. The Verma Committee (1999) also recommended measures on Fundamental Duties. Additionally, the 86th Amendment duty was added without a specific committee. Statement 1 is NOT correct.
Statement 2: 'All recommendations' were accepted — false. Tax duty and penal provisions were not enacted. The Committee proposed 8 duties; 10 were enacted. Statement 2 is NOT correct.
Statement 3: The 42nd Amendment did insert 'Socialist' and 'Secular' into the Preamble — this is correct. Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 2 are NOT correct — select option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in Statement 1 uses 'only body ever' — a claim too strong to be correct. Students who know the Swaran Singh Committee's central role in recommending duties may not pause to verify whether other bodies also made recommendations, accepting 'only' without scrutiny. Statement 2 uses 'all recommendations' — another scope-extension trap exploiting students who know some recommendations were adopted.
solution.final_explanation:
Precise knowledge of the Swaran Singh Committee's role and the 42nd Amendment's scope is required here.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The claim that the Swaran Singh Committee was the 'only body ever' to recommend additions to Fundamental Duties is false. The Verma Committee (1999) recommended implementation and could have recommended new duties. Furthermore, the 86th Amendment (2002) added a duty legislatively without any specific committee recommendation.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Committee's recommendations were selectively adopted. Tax-payment duty, penal provisions, and an 8-duty structure were all proposed but not enacted. Parliament chose 10 duties, adding some the Committee had not explicitly recommended.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The 42nd Amendment is indeed responsible for both the insertion of Part IV-A (Fundamental Duties) and the amendment of the Preamble to include 'Socialist' and 'Secular'. These were among several sweeping changes made by this single amendment.

Value Addition:
• The 42nd Amendment also inserted the word 'integrity' into the Preamble (to 'unity and integrity').
• The 44th Amendment (1978) reversed many 42nd Amendment changes but left the Preamble amendments and Part IV-A intact.
• The Preamble amendments (42nd) were upheld as valid in Kesavananda Bharati's aftermath.

solution.concept_anchor: Bijoe Emmanuel case — correct case-principle pairing
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) attributes the environmental PIL principle to the Bijoe Emmanuel case, which is a real case on Fundamental Duties — making it a sophisticated entity-swap trap.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): Bijoe Emmanuel (1986) concerned national anthem and religious freedom — not environmental duties. Attributing environmental PIL development to this case is an entity-swap.

Eliminate (c): AIIMS Students Union v. AIIMS (2001) involved 51A(j) — excellence and merit — not the principle that Fundamental Duties can override Fundamental Rights. That principle was rejected in Bijoe Emmanuel.

Eliminate (d): M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987) used 51A(g) to support environmental PILs — not the proposition that Fundamental Duties serve as aids to statutory interpretation (which is from AIIMS Students Union 2001).
Retain (b): Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala (1986) established that Fundamental Rights take precedence over Fundamental Duties in cases of conflict — the correct case-principle pairing.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Options (a), (c), and (d) all pair real cases with real Fundamental Duties principles — but with entity-swaps. The test requires students to know which principle was established in which specific case. Students who know 'Bijoe Emmanuel = Fundamental Duties' but are uncertain about the specific holding may accept option (a), which pairs it with an environmental principle from M.C. Mehta.
solution.final_explanation:
Case-principle pairing for Fundamental Duties requires knowing both the case and the precise legal principle it established.

• Option (a): Incorrect. Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala (1986) did not deal with environmental rights. This is an entity-swap — the environmental PIL principle comes from M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987).
• Option (b): Correct. Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala (1986) directly established that when a Fundamental Duty (51A(a) — respect national anthem) conflicts with a Fundamental Right (Articles 19, 25 — freedom of religion), the Fundamental Right prevails. Rights are constitutionally superior to duties.
• Option (c): Incorrect. AIIMS Students Union v. AIIMS (2001) used Article 51A(j) in the context of merit-based PG admissions — it did not establish that Fundamental Duties can override Fundamental Rights (the opposite was established in Bijoe Emmanuel).
• Option (d): Incorrect. M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987) used Article 51A(g) to support environmental PILs — not the statutory interpretation principle (which was established in AIIMS Students Union 2001).

Value Addition:
• Bijoe Emmanuel: Rights > Duties in conflict.
• AIIMS Students Union: Duties usable for statutory interpretation.
• M.C. Mehta: 51A(g) + 48A = constitutional environmental framework.

statement_analysis.reason: The Swaran Singh Committee recommended a duty to pay taxes, but it was not enacted. No duty to vote appears in Article 51A. Constitutions of other democracies include such civic duties.

statement_analysis.statement: Since Fundamental Duties cannot be enforced through judicial proceedings, Parliament has no constitutional authority to enact laws that penalise conduct violating a Fundamental Duty.
statement_analysis.reason: Parliament's legislative power is separate from Article 51A's non-justiciability. Multiple statutes (Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, Wildlife Protection Act) effectively enforce Fundamental Duties through penal provisions.

Statement 3 is incorrect: Parliament retains full authority to legislate — non-justiciability bars direct writ enforcement only. Existing statutes already penalise duty-violating conduct.
Statements 1 and 2 are correct, Statement 3 is incorrect — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is a partial-truth trap: it correctly states that Fundamental Duties cannot be enforced through judicial proceedings (writ jurisdiction), but incorrectly extends this to bar parliamentary legislation. The error is conflating constitutional non-justiciability with a bar on Parliament's legislative power to enforce duty-aligned conduct. These operate on entirely different planes of constitutional law.
solution.final_explanation:
The limitations of Fundamental Duties as enacted reveal important gaps in India's civic duty framework.

• Statement 1 — Correct: No duty to vote or pay taxes is found in Article 51A, despite these being fundamental civic obligations in many democracies. The Swaran Singh Committee recommended the tax duty; Parliament did not enact it.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The citizen-exclusivity of Fundamental Duties is a textual limitation. Non-citizens and corporations are exempt, whereas some rights (Articles 14, 20, 21) extend universally to persons.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Parliament is fully empowered to legislate on any subject giving effect to Fundamental Duties. The Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act (1971) and Wildlife Protection Act (1972) are examples of penal statutes reinforcing duties. Non-justiciability of Article 51A itself does not constrain Parliament's Article 246 legislative power.

Value Addition:
• The Verma Committee (1999) recommended making duties more effective through existing legislation — not new duty-specific statutes.
• Jury duty, community service, and compulsory national service are examples of civic duties in other constitutions absent from Article 51A.
• Duties apply to natural persons who are citizens — NRIs holding OCI cards are not citizens and thus not subject to Article 51A.
